transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in today? How can I help you?

I came in because I’m just… tired all the time. Not just normal “I had a busy day” tired, but like I’m running out of gas way too early. By midmorning at work, even if all I’ve really done is review claim files or walk one of the junior adjusters through a case, I feel like my body and my brain are already running on empty.

It’s frustrating because those are things I know how to do—I’ve been doing this kind of work for years—so it’s not like it’s physically demanding in the usual sense. But I’ll be sitting there trying to focus on details, estimates, notes, the sequence of events, and I just feel drained, like I’m pushing through mud. I guess I’m here because it’s gotten to where I can’t just brush it off as being busy or getting older.
Do you feel this way most days, or does it come and go?

Most days, yes. I mean, it’s not like I never have a slightly better morning here or there, but overall it’s pretty constant. By midmorning at work I’m already feeling wiped out, even if I’ve only been doing routine stuff like reviewing claim files or helping one of the junior adjusters think through a claim.

That’s the part that bothers me—it isn’t after some huge, stressful event or a twelve-hour day. It happens after things that should be manageable for me. I’ll be sitting there with the file open, going through notes and details, and it just feels like my body and my brain are both running on empty way too early in the day.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, or that you’ve lost interest in activities you used to like?

Yeah… I have, although I don’t know if I would have called it “lost interest” at first. It felt more like I was just trying to conserve energy and get through the workweek, and then everything else started dropping off.

At work, I’ve noticed I’m not as sharp as I used to be. In audits, I’ll miss little details that I normally would have caught, and then I have to go back over things again. Signing off on files takes me longer because I keep second-guessing myself or rereading the same parts to make sure I didn’t overlook something. And then by the time I get home, the idea of doing anything I used to enjoy feels like one more task.

I used to paint—not professionally or anything, just for myself—and I used to hike when I could, and I volunteered too. Those were things that made me feel like I had a life outside of claim files and deadlines. But lately I’ve pulled back from all of that. I tell myself, “Maybe next weekend,” or “once this week is over,” but then the next week feels the same, and I just end up doing the bare minimum to get by.
Do you feel down or depressed most of the day, nearly every day, not just during work or when you're tired?

Yeah… I think so. It’s not only at work or only when I’m tired, although work definitely makes it more obvious because I’m trying to function and keep up.

But even on days when nothing is really wrong, I feel like there’s this gray film over everything. Like I can be home, and my husband is being kind, or we’re cooking with the family, and I know on some level that those should be warm, good moments. I can laugh at the right time, I can help chop vegetables, I can sit at the table and be present enough that no one would necessarily think anything is wrong. But inside it feels muted. Like I’m going through the motions without really feeling the enjoyment the way I used to.

It’s hard to explain because I’m not always crying or anything dramatic like that. It’s more this steady heaviness, or dullness, most days. Even when things around me are okay, I still feel… down, I guess. Like the color’s been turned down on everything.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep—like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or sleeping much more than usual?

I’m not really sure how to answer that clearly. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed one obvious pattern, like “I can’t fall asleep every night” or “I’m sleeping all day,” if that’s what you mean.

I do think about sleep a lot, because when I wake up I often don’t feel especially refreshed, but I don’t know if that’s the sleep itself or just… the general way I’ve been feeling. Some nights I’m in bed at a normal time and I’m just sort of lying there, not exactly wide awake in a dramatic way, but not fully settled either. Other nights I think I sleep, at least enough hours on paper, but it doesn’t feel like it really restores me.

So I guess I haven’t noticed a big change that I can point to confidently. It’s more that sleep doesn’t seem to fix the tiredness the way I would expect it to.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating less than usual or losing weight without trying?

I don’t think I’ve noticed anything major there. My appetite is maybe a little inconsistent, but I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly been eating a lot less or losing weight without trying.

I mean, some days food just feels kind of… practical, like something I have to do because it’s dinnertime, not because I’m really looking forward to it. But I still eat. If my husband makes something, or if we’re having dinner with the family, I’ll have a normal plate, more or less. I haven’t had that thing where clothes are suddenly loose or people are commenting on my weight.

So, no, not really a weight loss or appetite change that stands out to me. At least not one I’d feel confident calling a real change.
Have you found yourself feeling like a failure or blaming yourself for things more than usual, even when it doesn’t seem entirely fair?

I don’t know that I’d say that’s a big thing for me. I mean… I can be hard on myself, sure, especially if I feel like I’m not keeping up or if I’ve made some mistake, but I’m not sure it’s more than usual or that I’m constantly thinking, “I’m a failure.”

It’s more like I’ll replay things sometimes and wonder if I handled them badly, or if I should have done more, or been more patient, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. I wouldn’t say I’m blaming myself for everything, exactly. I don’t walk around thinking everything is my fault.

So… maybe some self-criticism, but not in a way that stands out to me as the main issue. At least I haven’t noticed it as clearly as that.
Have you noticed yourself moving more slowly than usual, or feeling restless and unable to sit still, more than you used to?

I’m not sure I’ve noticed that, no. I mean, I know what you’re describing—like if someone is pacing all the time or people are asking why they’re moving so slowly—but I don’t think anyone has said that to me, and I haven’t really caught myself doing it in an obvious way.

At work, I still get up, go where I need to go, do the basic things at a normal enough pace, I think. Sometimes I probably sit longer than I should before starting something, but I’m not sure that’s “moving slowly” in the way you mean. And I don’t think I feel restless like I can’t sit still. If anything, I can sit still maybe too easily, but I wouldn’t call that the same thing.

So… no, not a clear change. I haven’t noticed my body feeling sped up or slowed down in a way that stands out.
How long have you been feeling this way—this constant tiredness, loss of enjoyment, and feeling down most of the time?

It’s been… a long time, honestly. I’d say about three years, maybe a little over that—around three years and three months, if I’m trying to be precise.

It started when I was moved into that higher-responsibility role at work, where I was mentoring other adjusters and helping oversee the new workflow systems. At first I thought it was just the stress of the change, like, “Okay, this is a bigger role, I just need to adjust and get used to it.” But it never really lifted. It just kind of became the normal background of my life.

So yes, since then—about three years and three months—it’s been there most of the time.
Have you ever felt so down or hopeless that you’ve thought about hurting yourself or that life isn’t worth living?

I… I don’t think so, not in that way. I mean, I’ve definitely had times where I feel really worn down and kind of wonder how I’m supposed to keep doing everything like this, but I don’t sit there thinking I want to hurt myself.

And “life isn’t worth living” is… that’s a strong phrase. I wouldn’t say I’ve had that thought exactly. It’s more like feeling tired of feeling tired, if that makes sense, or wishing things didn’t feel so heavy all the time. But I haven’t made any plans or thought about harming myself.

I guess I’d say no, not really. I feel low, but not like I’m at the point of wanting to hurt myself.

inference_history.note: The patient endorsed persistent fatigue, anhedonia (loss of interest in previously enjoyable activities), and decreased functioning at work with cognitive difficulties (e.g., trouble concentrating, missing details, rereading information). These symptoms are consistent with major depressive disorder, current episode (F32) or recurrent depressive disorder (F33). The severity could not yet be narrowed based on this turn. F48.0 (depressive disorder, not otherwise specified) and R53.81 (other fatigue) are ruled out due to sufficient symptom criteria now being met for a primary depressive disorder.

This turn ruled out F32.0 and F33.0 due to the patient's report of a persistent depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day, not limited to work or fatigue, which supports the presence of a depressed mood as a core symptom. The lack of clear changes in psychomotor activity rules out F32.0 and F33.0, which require fewer symptoms to meet the threshold for mild depression. The remaining candidates reflect moderate to severe depression with the presence of multiple core symptoms.

The chronic duration of symptoms (over 3 years) supports the diagnosis of recurrent depressive disorder. The lack of clear changes in self-esteem, psychomotor disturbance, or guilt makes more severe categories less likely.
